A content delivery network is a system that helps websites and apps load quickly no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, every request for a photo, video, or webpage travels back to a single origin server — the original computer that stores the real, master copy of that content. If that server sits far away, the trip takes noticeable time, and popularity spikes can overwhelm it. A content delivery network solves this by copying content onto many smaller computers scattered around the world, each called an edge location, because it sits at the "edge" of the network, close to where people actually are. When a request arrives, it goes to the nearest edge location instead of the distant origin. If that location already has a saved copy ready to serve, this is called a cache hit, and the content appears almost instantly. If not, the edge location fetches a copy from the origin server once, saves it, and serves it faster to everyone after that. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep copies of popular books, so readers do not have to travel to one central library every time. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out traffic so no single server gets overloaded, and keeps services running smoothly even during sudden surges of visitors. In short, spreading copies closer to the audience is the whole trick behind fast, reliable delivery across the internet.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer holding the master copy of content | Every new or updated file ultimately comes from here |
| Edge location | A local computer positioned close to visitors | Shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered instantly from a saved copy | Makes loading fast and reduces strain on the origin server |
| Cache miss | A request not found nearby that must be fetched from the origin | Slower the first time, but the copy is saved for next time |
